title: 2026-12-21 onprem airgapped GPU drivers offline licensing artifact delivery technical deep dive
meeting_header:
Date: 2026-12-21
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim, Priya Desai, Jordan Liu (Redwood) — Mark Thompson, Sarah Patel, Liam O'Connor, Elena Ruiz (GreenWave)
summary: Deep dive on on-prem air-gapped deployment requirements: artifact delivery process, offline licensing for GPU drivers, driver packaging, runtime performance (latency/throughput), KV cache/continuous batching, quantization options and tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: share offline licensing guide and driver packaging checklist, schedule 2-week pilot for benchmarking, provide estimated Dedicated/Private pricing and security docs.

transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll cover the artifact delivery and offline licensing flow, plus runtime perf questions. Priya and I are from Redwood, Jordan is on for CSM and followups.
[00:15] Mark: Thanks, appreciate you fitting this in. We have a pretty tight compliance window so want to make sure the air-gap path is clean.
[00:30] Priya: Great, quick agenda: artifact bundle contents, checksums/signing, offline license key distribution for GPU drivers, driver install order, and then we dig into runtime perf: kv cache, batching, quant, latency/throughput.
[00:45] Sarah: Quick note — our infra is on premise, isolated network, we can do physical media transfers but need chain-of-custody logs. Also we use RHEL 8.8 and NVIDIA A100 nodes, 80GB.
[01:05] Alex: Perfect. We support signed artifact bundles that include model weights, runtime binaries, and a driver package. For air-gapped, we produce a tar.gz with a signed manifest plus a detached GPG signature. The manifest lists checksums SHA256.
[01:25] Liam: Who holds the private signing key? We require we verify signatures with a public key we control.
[01:35] Priya: Redwood will sign; we can also provide a hash and you can verify locally. If you want, we can do dual signing: Redwood and a third-party escrow. But typically customers verify our public key; we can rotate per-transfer.
[01:50] Elena: What about driver licensing — Nvidia driver binary packages require offline license activation in our environment; how does Redwood handle that?
[02:05] Alex: We don't re-license vendor drivers, we package them and provide offline license tokens where required. For some OEMs, the driver has separate offline activation — we provide step-by-step and the license blob. For customers who manage their own driver licensing, we can omit driver blobs and only provide runtime + model.
[02:25] Priya: To be concrete: our artifact bundle contains (1) runtime tar (redwood-runtime-vX.Y.Z), (2) model weights tar, (3) optional gpu-driver tar, (4) installation scripts, (5) manifest.sha256 + manifest.sig, (6) offline-license.json (encrypted). We also include instructions for NCCL/OS kernel modules order.
[02:50] Mark: Are the drivers pre-built for your kernel versions? We have custom kernel patches for our environment.
[03:05] Priya: We can provide both pre-built driver binaries for common kernels and the driver source package for you to build. Build instructions and expected kernel config flags are in the package. For validated installs we recommend matching the driver major version we tested — we provide the exact driver version used in our performance tests.
[03:25] Sarah: Which driver versions are you validating with?
[03:30] Alex: Our current stable run used NVIDIA driver 525.85. For A100 80GB we also validate with 530.x series in our internal tests. We'll include the exact kernel module versions in the manifest.
[03:45] Liam: For security audits we need the SHA of any binary blobs and a reproducible build path. Is the build container available?
[03:55] Priya: We provide a hermetic build container image (OCI tar) that you can import offline; it contains the toolchain and scripts to reproduce the driver build and the runtime packaging. The container image is signed and checksummed.
[04:15] Mark: Ok good. Now on runtime perf — our SLO target is p95 latency <= 350ms for short chat requests (avg 50 tokens) and throughput of ~200 concurrent streams. Is that realistic on A100 nodes?
[04:35] Priya: Depends on model and quantization. For, say, a Llama-2-13B style arch, with q4_0 quant and continuous KV cache and optimized kernels, a single A100 80GB with batching can handle maybe 100-150 concurrent short streams with p95 near 300-400ms; for 200 streams you either need dedicated pools or batching/serving across multiple GPUs. If you accept int8 or q4_K that helps throughput but might affect quality.
[05:05] Mark: We have stricter quality constraints; can't accept notable drift. We want to measure tradeoffs.
[05:15] Priya: Right; our Optimize module suggests quant profiles per workload. For retrieval-augmented chat where you append docs, sequence lengths vary; prefix KV caching is essential to avoid re-calculating prefix attention. We typically enable prefix K-V cache for 95% of flows and set cache TTLs.
[05:35] Elena: Can you explain the KV cache impact in practice?
[05:40] Priya: Sure — with KV caching, if you have a repeated system prompt or retrieved context, we avoid recomputing attention keys/values for the prefix. That reduces per-token compute and latency. It also affects memory per request (we store KV per active session) and eviction policies influence throughput.
[06:00] Sarah: Do you support sharded KV across GPUs?
[06:05] Priya: Yes, across multi-GPU nodes we shard the KV by head group; runtime coordinates retrieval. For on-prem we recommend pinning sessions to the same GPU when latency-critical, or using a multi-GPU partitioning strategy if you need higher throughput.
[06:25] Alex: Also continuous batching: we group tokens across inflight sessions within a micro-batch window — tradeoff between added queuing latency and improved GPU utilization. We recommend dynamic batching with a short tail latency budget (e.g., 8-12ms micro batching) to hit throughput targets.
[06:45] Mark: For our use-case we can't accept >20ms extra headroom; what do you recommend?
[06:50] Priya: Start with micro-batch window 8ms and a max batch size configured per model/hardware. We can run a profile during pilot and tune. Also, you can use prioritized queues for production traffic to avoid tail latency on important requests.
[07:05] Liam: On quantization: what formats do you support and what's the expected quality delta?
[07:10] Priya: We support standard int8 and several low-bit formats like q4_0 and q4_K (model dependent). For many workloads q4_K gives near-fp16 quality with big memory savings. We run evaluation suites against your prompts to produce a quality vs throughput curve. Usually q4_0 is safe for non-critical outputs; q4_K is a better sweet spot for chat.
[07:35] Elena: Do we need to recompile kernels for quantized execution (TensorRT or custom kernels)?
[07:40] Priya: For the most optimized path we use a combination: custom CUDA kernels for attention and matmuls and optional TensorRT for fusion. No OS kernel compile required; CUDA and NCCL versions must match driver stacks. TensorRT gives additional speed but is an optional runtime path.
[08:00] Mark: Any known gotchas for A100 80GB with 530 drivers and CUDA 12.x?
[08:05] Priya: On some distros the 530.x driver + CUDA 12 had changes to peer-to-peer that required NCCL tuning; we include recommended NCCL env vars in the package. Also ensure MIG isn't enabled if you're planning to use whole-GPU scheduling.
[08:25] Sarah: About offline licensing for runtime — is that per-node or per-cluster?
[08:30] Alex: Licensing model is flexible: offline key can be per-node (bind to hardware fingerprint) or per-cluster (consumption-based). For strict air-gap customers we often do node-bound keys with a renewal window; we send encrypted license blobs signed by our licensing authority and you apply them via a local activation CLI.
[08:50] Liam: We need audit trails for activations. Can activation events be logged to local syslog and exported to our SIEM?
[08:55] Priya: Yes, activations generate a verifiable event record; we provide an activation log file and optional syslog integration. Logs include timestamp, node fingerprint, license id (hashed) and signing fingerprint.
[09:15] Mark: On artifact delivery chaining — what is the expected lead time to generate a bundle and the logistics?
[09:20] Alex: Typically 3-5 business days to prepare a signed artifact bundle for a new model and driver combination. If you need a rebuild for a custom kernel it can be 7-10 days. We use tracked couriers for USB drives or can provide an encrypted ship-and-seal approach with an HSM partner.
[09:45] Elena: For the pilot we prefer to do a dry-run via our staging isolated cluster first. Can you provide a smaller sample bundle for staging?
[09:55] Priya: Absolutely — we provide a trimmed bundle with a small model sample and runtime to validate install paths — no licensing required for the sample. Full model bundle is gated.
[10:10] Mark: Ok, performance testing — what telemetry do you collect in air-gapped setups?
[10:15] Priya: By default the runtime emits local metrics (prometheus textfile or pushgateway) and tracing data (Jaeger-compatible spans) which you keep onsite. For hosted customers we ingest telemetry centrally; for private we provide the same schema and dashboards so you can run the same queries.
[10:35] Sarah: Do you collect any PII in telemetry? Need to ensure we can scrub or disable fields.
[10:40] Priya: Telemetry is configurable — request/response payloads are not collected by default. You can enable or disable fields; we support token-level redaction and exclude raw payloads for compliance.
[10:55] Mark: About failover — if a GPU node becomes unavailable in on-prem, do you have graceful fallbacks?
[11:00] Alex: Yes, our serving layer supports automatic fallback to a smaller model or to a remote Dedicated pool if networking allows — in air-gapped that remote fallback won't be available. Locally we recommend a small standby pool sized for critical routes, or pre-warmed CPU fallback which is slower but keeps service up.
[11:20] Liam: For the license renewal process — if connectivity to Redwood is impossible, how do we renew?
[11:25] Alex: We support time-limited offline renewal tokens via an out-of-band process. You present the node fingerprint and receive a signed renewal blob that you apply locally. Renewal windows can be long (e.g., yearly) to minimize transfers.
[11:40] Elena: Can we automate the apply of license via Ansible?
[11:45] Priya: Yes, the activation CLI is scriptable and idempotent; we include example Ansible tasks in the bundle.
[11:55] Mark: Let's talk about benchmarking plan for the pilot. We'll need to run p50/p95/p99 curves across a synthetic traffic mix and also with real retrieval-augmented prompts.
[12:10] Priya: We'll provide a benchmarking harness (Python) that runs locally, collects metrics, and writes standardized CSVs. We also include a template for ramping concurrent sessions and varying micro-batching windows. In pilot we usually run three runs: baseline fp16, q4_0, q4_K.
[12:35] Sarah: How do you measure perplexity/quality during quant runs?
[12:40] Priya: We run your evaluation prompts through each config and compute n-gram overlap, embedding similarity, and custom evaluation metrics you define (e.g., business-rule match). We'll produce a quality-vs-throughput report.
[12:55] Lara: [crosstalk/unknown] — sorry, who is Lara?
[12:58] Jordan: That's my mistaken background noise, ignore.
[13:05] Mark: Any special network config for on-prem? We have strict egress rules so the runtime must start with no external calls.
[13:12] Priya: Runtime supports fully offline start; we include a policy file that disables outbound telemetry and remote fetches. For licensing checks you either use offline license or have a scheduled maintenance window for inbound validation.
[13:30] Liam: On cryptographic side — are the offline license blobs encrypted with customer public key?
[13:35] Alex: We encrypt license blobs with your public key by default, then sign with Redwood's private key. You control decryption locally.
[13:45] Elena: For the driver install order — any gotchas for kernel module loading?
[13:50] Priya: Yes: install kernel headers, then driver, then NCCL and CUDA runtime, then runtime. We include scripts that check module dependencies and verify symbol versions. For RHEL variants ensure kernel-devel matches running kernel.
[14:10] Sarah: If we need custom tuning (NCCL env vars, memalign), do you assist?
[14:15] Priya: Yes, as part of pilot we'll propose tuned env vars, e.g., NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME, NCCL_IB_HCA, and memlock limits. We can remote into your staging environment (with customer-controlled keys and jump hosts) to observe and suggest changes during the bench run.
[14:35] Mark: Any legal constraints on shipping driver binaries?
[14:40] Alex: Usually drivers come with vendor EULAs; we include the license text and require acceptance. For some vendors an explicit customer agreement is required. We'll coordinate legal with your procurement.
[14:55] Elena: Ok, recap and next steps?
[15:00] Alex: Recap: we'll send offline licensing guide, driver packaging checklist, sample artifact bundle for staging, benchmarking harness, and security docs. You (GreenWave) will confirm pilot dates and share SLOs/dataset samples.
[15:15] Mark: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[15:20] Jordan: I'll follow up with calendar invites for the pilot and a link to the shared secure transfer checklist.
[15:25] End of recording.
